Bardiches are a combination axe and spear, so you need to learn how to make both, so you can incorporate elements of both into the design. For the axe portion, start with a simple design, like a hatchet. Once you're pumping those out confidently, start experimenting with more elaborate designs. Most importantly, if you want to make a bardiche, you need to learn how to extend the beard and flare the heel, like a bearded axe. This is important, as you need to learn how to forge the heel so it doesn't chip or snap after a hard blow, since that curve between the cheek and the heel is potential weak point if not forged properly. This practice will also help you with extending the toe and cheek to form the spearhead portion of the bardiche. Practice making some dane axes, as their much more gentle cheek slope and shorter extension on the toe is a good starting point to branch out from.

At the same time, start making arrowheads, since they're essentially tiny spearheads. Stick with a simple, diamond-head design, Once you get that down, work your way up to full-size spearheads. Then start experimenting a little. Start flaring the base and flattening the spine to make leaf and boar spears (and broad-head arrows, don't stop making arrowheads just cause you've moved on to spears). Start extending the point to make pikes and pig stickers (and bodkin arrows). Once you can forge a narrow, spike-tipped spear 6 to 8 inches long that won't snap under pressure, you're ready to combine your talents and make a bardiche.

For the final forging of the bardiche, you need to strengthen the metal in three different directions. Firstly, it obviously needs to be able to take abuse along the hardened bit, transferring energy into the softer, more resilient cheek. Second, it needs to be able to channel pressure down through the heel and beard to the shaft. Third, the toe and upper cheek needs to be formed into a spearhead with a hardened tip and edges to punch into the target, but with a resilient spine to handle lateral pressures without snapping.
